extracted_by: hand, T-0312 — the Democrat read, March 1834
note: Vol. I No. 15, and the issue that explains the hole in this month: it carries a dateline of Saturday, March 8 over a March 4 nameplate, says the number was held back for the Ottawa convention, and announces that the Democrat will be suspended for want of paper. It also carries the month's only post-office letter list, on page 4 — a list no earlier sweep found, because the segmenter cut its heading across a column boundary.

claims.notes: THE DEMOCRAT SUSPENDS ITSELF FOR WANT OF PAPER, and this is why March 1834 holds three issues and not four. The paper says it will be discontinued for a few weeks, names the cause — its stock of paper was insufficient for the winter and the printers had only lately concluded to settle here — and records the remedy: Doct. J. T. Temple, one of the proprietors of the line of stages from St Louis, carried an arrangement for a supply by stage, which had not yet arrived because of the state of the roads. The Democrat of 1834-03-18 (claim c001 there) reports the supply received and the publication resumed. Read with c002 below — this number is itself datelined Saturday, March 8 over a March 4 nameplate — the two together answer the question T-0312 was written to ask: the Democrat skipped the week, the deposit has no hole. The masthead numbering agrees, 1834-03-18 being Vol. I No. 16 and not No. 17. The segmenter alternates this column with the Missouri Republican's counterfeiter descriptions line by line; lines_of_claim names the lines the notice can be followed through.

We had purposely and from other reasons delayed the publication of the present number of the Democrat, in order to lay before our rea[?]ders the proceedings of the Convention held at [Ottawa on the 3d] […] [We a]re sorry that we are obl[ig]ed to defer t[he] publication of the Address, owing to its length and the late hour at which it was received — […] as we shall receive a supply of paper. [We shall lay it before] our readers no soo[ner than] […]
claims.notes: THE NUMBER DATED MARCH 4 WAS PRINTED ON OR AFTER MARCH 8, in the paper's own words and over its own dateline, and it says why twice: it was held back for the Ottawa convention of 3-5 March, and the address it means to print must wait until a supply of paper arrives. That is the same shortage c001 announces the suspension for. A reconstruction should not read the 1834 Democrat's nameplate date as a printing date without checking the column: 1834-03-04 and 1834-03-18 are eight and eighteen days apart on the nameplate but the interval the town actually went without a paper is longer at one end and shorter at the other.

claims.notes: THE FIRST SIDEWALK THE TOWN ORDERED, AND IT IS DIMENSIONED: ten feet wide, gravel or brick, with two-inch oak curbing, in front of every lot on South Water Street between the United States reservation and Randolph Street, to the pitch set by the town surveyor, complete by 1 July 1834 — one year to the day before the scene date, and at the owners' expense if they did not. This is a dated floor for the South Water frontage the walkthrough shows, and it is an ORDER rather than a report: it says what the Trustees required, not what was built, and the gate between the two is the reason nothing here should be promoted past `documented` for the walk's existence in 1835. The meeting sat at Dexter Graves's house, which the same issue's blacksmith advertisement (c021) uses as the anchor for Graves' Tavern on Main-street.

One third of the timber must be delivered at the Piers by the 15th of April next, and the other two [th]ir[ds], during that month. claims.notes: THE PIERS OF THE CHICAGO HARBOR, BILLED OUT IN SCANTLINGS, sixteen months before the scene date. The agent wants 10,000 feet of squared oak a foot square, in equal thirds of 30-, 25- and 20-foot logs; 350 round logs for ties, 24 feet and squaring about 11 inches; and 50 round white oak piles 25 feet long squaring at least 12 inches. One third to be at the Piers by 15 April 1834 and the rest within the month, with poplar or soft wood bought to float the oak rafts. For a reconstruction this is the pier's own material specification rather than an impression of it, and it dates the second season of the works: the Engineer's report read in January 1834 (1834-01-21 c001) says almost nothing had been built, and by August 1834 the North Pier is crossing the bar. THE 1834-03-18 REPRINT READS SOME OF THE NUMBERS DIFFERENTLY — 50-foot logs for 30, 40 piles for 50, 29 feet for 25 — and that issue's claim c011 records the variance rather than choosing between them; both columns are Tesseract fallbacks and neither reading is senior. The signature is 'Many, ALLEN' here and 'J. ALLEN' on 1834-03-18, which is why the agent is given as J. Allen and not expanded further.

So the contradiction is against the FIRM Brewster, Hogan & Co., which stops here, and not against the storefront, which the same issue independently locates: Collins & Caton advertise their office as one door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co. on South Water-street (c018), still using the old firm's name as the town's landmark for the place a fortnight after the dissolution. claims.normalized: FOR THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT. Mr. E[di]tor — Permit me the grateful priv[i]lege of making a few remarks upon a subject interwoven with the duties of our public and domestic life. In doing so, I would make al[l] [pos]sible allowance for the recent [dis]locations in th[i]s place. But, while our town officers are [m]aking law[s] a[n]d expending money (I admit) for [u]seful p[u]rposes, should not the fact [I] am about to lay befo[re my] fellow citizens, come under their cognizance? The removal of the coffin[s] projecting from the bank of the Lake, and the enclo[sing of the buri]al ground belonging to this town. [The] situation of the grave yard is [af]fronting to human [natu]re […]
claims.notes: COFFINS PROJECTING FROM THE BANK OF THE LAKE, in March 1834, in a signed letter asking the town officers to remove them and to enclose the burial ground. This is a lakeshore condition rather than a building, and it is filed as `building` because the burial ground is the thing being asked for — the vocabulary has no `ground` kind. What it is good for is a date: the town's lake-bank burying ground was still unenclosed and still eroding into the lake sixteen months before the scene date. It says nothing about where the ground was, and nothing here should be read as placing it; the letter's own later lines are cut to single words by the segmenter and are not claimed. The lines are woven with the canal land-grant bill beside them.

The business here is a PREMISES and not a firm — the paper names no proprietor and none is invented — so the gazetteer entry is a placed storefront with an empty proprietor list, which is the honest shape. The corpus README's count of letter lists in T-0258's thirty issues names 1834-01-28, 1834-02-04, 1834-04-23 and 1834-04-30 and NOT this issue, and the reason is mechanical: the heading is cut across a segmenter column boundary, 'List of L' ending page 4 column 2's first line and 'ost-Offiee at Chica-' opening column 3, so no line in the file contains 'list of letters' or 'post office' and every keyword sweep ran straight past it. WHAT SURVIVES IS SURNAMES: the segmenter cut this column at the left edge, so most entries reach the file with the forename gone — 'ell Baldwin', 'nel Devoe', 'il. Frazer'. Five names in this half carry a forename or initials legible enough to key on and only those five are minted; the rest are quoted and left unminted, because a bare surname is not a name and the gazetteer keys on the whole one. Nineteen lines of the printed list survive in this half. The count and the damage are stated in the PR and a ticket is opened for a page-image read.

Johnson', 'c Killigoss'. Three names carry enough to key on and are minted; the rest are recorded and not minted, on the rule that a bare surname is not a name. The count that matters for ruling 1 is therefore a FLOOR of 78 surviving list lines across both halves — nineteen here and fifty-nine there — against EIGHT minted, and the gap between them is a page-image read, not an estimate. Two entries the transcription does carry are worth naming for the town: '|.
